papers.title: One blood methylation profile stratifies ten-year risk across 21 common diseases
papers.abstract: Blood DNA methylation offers a dynamic readout of inherited and acquired influences on health, creating an opportunity for risk prediction beyond polygenic scores, which are fixed at conception and have yet to demonstrate broad clinical utility. As such, we aimed to develop methylation risk scores for 21 common diseases in 12,785 adults from Generation Scotland and the Mass General Brigham Biobank, combining technically reproducible probes, null-calibrated feature selection and ten-year survival models, with evaluation in a single holdout that was not used for feature selection, model fitting or tuning. The methylation risk scores for eight diseases reached a holdout C-index of at least 0.80: chronic kidney disease, peripheral vascular disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, heart failure and type 2 diabetes with at least 50 events each, and interstitial lung disease, dementia and fatty liver disease with fewer. For the five scores with at least 50 events, adjusted hazard ratios per standard deviation ranged from 2.6 to 4.1, with the highest risk tertile containing 73 to 90% of the ten-year events. Panel CpGs were enriched for cytokine signalling, innate immune sensing and sterol metabolism. Against reported values, the eight top-tier methylation risk scores exceed published polygenic and methylation scores alone, and exceed published polygenic and methylation scores that include clinical covariates for seven of the eight diseases (the exception is type 2 diabetes, where our AUC of 0.865 without clinical risk factors is close to a methylation-plus-risk-factor model at 0.872, and our C-index of 0.809 is lower than the C-index for a polygenic-plus-risk-factor at 0.85). These results indicate that a single blood methylation profile can rank ten-year risk for several common diseases at a level that compares favourably with published genetic and methylation scores.

papers.title: Rare copy number variation in alcohol use disorder using whole-genome sequencing in the All of Us Research Program
papers.abstract: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) is common, heritable (h2 ~50%) and polygenic, but the contribution of rare structural variation is largely unexamined. Using short-read whole-genome sequencing (srWGS) data from the All of Us Research Program, we tested the association of rare copy number variants (rCNV; minor allele frequency <1%) with AUD in 56,062 participants (5,410 cases, 50,652 controls) defined from electronic health records. Analyses were conducted within European-like (EUR; N=29,392), African-like (AFR; N=8,269) and Admixed American-like (AMR; N=8,049) samples and combined by cross-ancestry meta-analysis. We tested genome-wide rCNV burden, burden within AUD-related, mouse behavioral and neuropsychiatric gene sets, and individual rCNV regions. No genome-wide burden metric or individual rCNV region [≥]10 kb was associated with AUD after false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Significant gene-set results were almost exclusively duplications associated with reduced AUD risk across biologically unrelated sets, suggesting a global duplication dosage effect rather than pathway-specific enrichment. In contrast, deletion count within a Neurof_UnionStringent gene set was associated with increased AUD risk (OR=1.04, FDR=0.044), and deletions in xenobiotic-response genes showed nominal associations in multiple ancestry groups. Among rCNV of all sizes, a 58 bp deletion at 16p12.1, a dosage-sensitive neuropsychiatric locus, was significant in the cross-ancestry analysis (OR=2.93, FDR=0.030) without significant heterogeneity. rCNV detectable by srWGS do not appear to contribute substantially to AUD liability at current sample sizes.

papers.title: Brain Cell-Type-Specific X-Chromosome Gene Regulation Reveals Sex-Biased Candidate Genes in Neurodegeneration
papers.abstract: The impact of X-chromosome dosage on gene regulation in specific brain cell-types may importantly shape sex differences in neurodegenerative diseases but remains poorly resolved. We therefore mapped X-chromosome genetic effects on gene expression, i.e. cis-expression quantitative trait loci (cis-eQTL), across seven brain cell-types from 423 old-age individuals. We identified 212 X-linked genes whose expression was genetically regulated, with the majority being cell-type specific. Notably, 10 of these genes (~5%) showed sex-heterogeneous genetic regulation. Through sex-differential expression analyses we further discovered 101 sex-biased genes that were predominantly female-upregulated most strikingly in microglia. Sex-biased gene expression showed both shared and distinct cell-type effects, appearing most divergent in non-neuronal populations. Many female-biased genes overlapped known escape-from-X-inactivation genes and were enriched for links to Alzheimer's disease. Finally, we integrated our resource with X-chromosome-wide association studies of neurodegenerative diseases through causal inference approaches including transcriptome-wide association, mendelian randomization, and colocalization analyses to nominate 11 candidate causal genes, linked to their respective cell-types and sex-informed mechanisms, for Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and Multiple System Atrophy. Altogether, our findings suggest escape from X chromosome inactivation may contribute to sex differences in neurodegeneration and provide a resource to advance sex-informed insights into disease pathogenesis and therapeutic opportunities.

papers.title: Plasma Proteogenomic Uncovers Novel Molecular Mechanisms of Soluble Endoglin and Identifies AZI2 as a new Player in Arteriovenous Malformations in Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia
papers.abstract: Endoglin is a transmembrane glycoprotein that plays a key role in vascular development, angiogenesis and endothelial homeostasis. Its soluble form (Sol-ENG), generated through proteolytic shedding of the membrane-bound protein, has been implicated in the pathophysiology of numerous cardiovascular diseases, ranging from common conditions such as preeclampsia and thrombosis to rare diseases such as hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT). Leveraging large-scale genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics and metabolomics data from public and original resources, we identify a molecular signature of 24 markers associated with plasma levels of Sol-ENG. This signature was enriched in genes coding for GPI-enchored proteins and included metabolites participating to glycosylation and redox homeostasis. Furthermore, we observed that ABO blood groups and genetically predicted plasma levels of 5-Azacytidine Induced 2 (AZI2) associate with the risk of arteriovenous malformations in HHT patients. This study provides new insights into the physiological mechanisms underlying Endoglin regulation and opens clinical perspectives for the management of HHT patients.

papers.title: Promoter methylation of LDLR is not a common cause of familial hypercholesterolemia
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Familial hypercholesterolemia (FH) is a widely prevalent inherited disorder defined by chronically high LDL-C concentrations and a significantly increased risk of cardiovascular disease. While FH is primarily an autosomal dominant disease caused by pathogenic mutations in LDLR, APOB, or PCSK9, approximately 20-60% of clinically diagnosed patients are mutation-negative. A previous survey of over 23,000 methylation profiles identified a differentially methylated region in the promoter of LDLR. This study aimed to investigate whether constitutional hypermethylation of the LDLR promoter is a recurrent cause of FH in patients lacking identifiable pathogenic variants. Methods: We screened 308 mutation-negative clinically confirmed FH patients for promoter hypermethylation in LDLR. We used Combined Bisulfite Restriction Analysis (COBRA) with genomic DNA from peripheral blood samples. The assay assessed methylation at TaqI sites within a 332 bp region of the LDLR promoter. Results: No instances of LDLR promoter hypermethylation were detected among the 308 mutation-negative FH patients. Statistical analysis yielded an upper bound of 1.19% (95% Clopper-Pearson CI) for the prevalence of this specific epimutation in our cohort. Conclusions: Our results indicate that LDLR promoter hypermethylation at this specific locus is not a common cause of the FH phenotype in mutation-negative patients. These findings imply that while methylation in this region may be rare or not significantly contribute to the disease phenotype, the diagnostic gap in FH may be explained by other factors, such as methylation in other regions, polygenic risk, structural variants, or non-canonical regulatory mutations.

papers.title: Circulating immune architecture across age, exposures and disease in ethnically diverse UK cohorts.
papers.abstract: Human immune composition reflects genetic background and cumulative life-course exposures, yet how these influences shape immune architecture across populations and disease remains poorly understood. Here we integrate single-cell transcriptomics, matched clinical haematology and electronic health records from 5,079 individuals of European, British-Pakistani and British-Bangladeshi ancestries to quantify 26 circulating immune cell types and 62 transcriptional states. We map immune compositional variation associated with age, sex, adiposity and smoking, revealing distinct patterns across adulthood and associations between modifiable exposures and advanced immune age. Across common diseases, immune compositional signatures converge on recurrent inflammatory myeloid, adaptive-memory and interferon programmes, whose expression varies with age and population context. Cardiovascular therapies are associated with selective shifts in disease-associated immune states. Immune composition further discriminates common cardiometabolic diseases and resolves patients into endotypes with distinct metabolic and clinical profiles. These findings establish circulating immune architecture as an integrative phenotype linking life-course exposures, population context and disease, providing a framework for precision population immunology.

papers.title: Hierarchical genetic regulatory architecture of the human immune system informs complex disease mechanisms
papers.abstract: How inherited genetic variation propagates through multicellular regulatory systems to influence human disease remains poorly understood. To reconstruct the regulatory architecture of genetic variation on circulating immune cells, we analysed single-cell transcriptomes from 6.7 million peripheral blood mononuclear cells from 4,452 European-ancestry UK Biobank participants, identifying 114,063 independent cis-regulatory effects affecting 15,419 genes. Using a new statistical workflow (FLANDERS), we map the hierarchical organisation of these effects and the underlying regulatory architecture across tissues, immune lineages, cell types and cell states. We find that disease-associated variants predominantly act through regulatory programmes shared within immune lineages and broad cellular compartments, rather than through highly specific cellular states. We show that local cis -regulatory effects commonly act through coherent regulatory pathways implicating transcription factor cascades and intercellular signalling, which allows linking together multiple disease genes. We demonstrate independent support for these genes and mechanisms through rare variant associations. Our findings reveal a highly organised structure of immune regulatory variation shaping human disease, and provide a highly effective framework for interpreting disease associations and prioritising therapeutic targets.

papers.title: Additional value of germline genomic scores beyond prostate-specific antigen alone for long-term and near-term prostate cancer risk
papers.abstract: We evaluated whether germline genomic risk complements prostate-specific antigen (PSA) for prostate cancer early detection. P-CARE integrates a 601-variant polygenic hazard score, family history, and genetic ancestry. Long-term outcomes and clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) detection on biopsy were assessed in the Million Veteran Program (MVP), with external validation in the Prostate Cancer Prevention Trial (PCPT). Among 428,512 MVP participants, high versus low P-CARE risk was associated with increased hazards of treatment (HR 3.32) and metastasis (HR 3.32). Among men whose baseline PSA was measured at ages 40-49 with PSA 1-3 ng/mL, 15-year treatment/metastasis probabilities were 2.6%, 4.5%, and 10.2% across increasing P-CARE risk groups. High P-CARE risk also predicted csPCa on biopsy (OR 2.96), while PRSPSA was inversely associated with outcomes. Findings were consistent in PCPT. Germline genomic risk complements measured PSA, supporting prospective evaluation of genetically informed screening strategies.

papers.title: MRCAT: A multi-agent framework for reliable Mendelian randomization analysis and causal interpretation
papers.abstract: Mendelian randomization (MR) uses genetic variants to estimate causal effects of exposures on health outcomes, but rigorous MR analyses require coordinated procedures and interpretation under explicit methodological assumptions. Although artificial intelligence (AI) agents can automate analyses, computational completion does not guarantee scientific reliability. Here, we present MRCAT, a multi-agent framework that translates MR-specific knowledge into an AI-assisted workflow that is plannable, executable, verifiable, recoverable and traceable. MRCAT combines dependency-aware planning, Skill-guided execution and expert-informed review with traceable reporting guided by STROBE-MR, a guideline for clear and transparent reporting of MR studies, and iterative Writer-Judge checking. We evaluated MRCAT on 30 natural-language queries spanning diverse data sources, analytical requirements and boundary conditions. MRCAT achieved scientific completion, defined as meeting all nine prespecified MR-specific procedural requirements, for all 26 executable queries and appropriately handled all four boundary cases, compared with 17, 11 and 4 scientifically completed queries for Claude Code, Biomni and BioMedAgent, respectively. Across six independently curated tasks for which the expert-curated analyses did not support causal effects, MRCAT showed closer numerical concordance with the expert-curated analyses and produced interpretations consistent with expert-curated conclusions in all six cases, compared with two for Claude Code and four for Biomni. Additional case studies demonstrated evidence-grounded reporting and selective reuse of analytical outputs in multi-exposure and bidirectional MR investigations. MRCAT provides a framework for reducing the operational burden of MR research while supporting reproducible analysis, assumption-consistent interpretation and traceable scientific reporting.

papers.title: Multimodal population-scale cell atlases define archetypes and extremes of human blood
papers.abstract: The cellular composition of blood is fundamental to human physiology and is routinely measured to assess health and disease. Circulating immune cells show extensive heterogeneity, but the organising principles and extremes of variation across individuals remain undefined. Here, using single-cell transcriptomics across two biobank cohorts encompassing ~6,000 individuals, we show that human blood occupies recurrent archetypal states defined by coordinated cell composition patterns. We delineate three major archetypes spanning naive lymphoid, myeloid and cytotoxic composition, and two minor archetypes characterised by type I interferon-driven inflammation and expanded premalignant CD5+ B cells. We develop cell2clone to infer lymphocyte clonal expansions, revealing how reactive clonal processes drive the cytotoxic archetype and premalignant clonal expansion establishes the CD5+ B cell archetype, creating outlier states that uncover context-specific effects of germline variants. Clonal haematopoiesis and mosaic chromosomal alterations influence blood states in an archetype-dependent manner. The archetype framework links blood states to common disease risk and clinical blood counts and, through a machine-learning model ArcheTypist, classifies infection and cancer immunotherapy outcomes. This population-scale framework has implications for diagnostics, early disease detection, immunotherapy stratification and mechanistic insights into disease susceptibility and therapy response, providing an organising model for identifying compositional subtypes across human tissues.

papers.title: Integrative Multi-Ancestry and Multi-Tissue Fine-Mapping Prioritizes Candidate Causal Genes for Risk of Breast Cancer and Its Subtypes
papers.abstract: Most breast cancer (BC) risk loci identified by genome wide association studies lie in noncoding regions, and traditional transcriptome-wide association studies (TWAS) often prioritize multiple correlated genes per locus. We applied two gene fine-mapping methods, TGVIS and M cTWAS, which jointly model gene expression, splicing and alternative polyadenylation (APA) with direct variant effects, to overall BC, estrogen receptor-negative (ER negative) BC and triple-negative BC (TNBC) in women of European and African ancestry. Using 11 BC-relevant GTEx v10 tissues, we prioritized 31, 13 and 5 candidate causal genes, respectively, in European-ancestry populations. Compared with marginal TWAS, fine-mapping reduced the number of candidate genes per locus by 72 to 88%, and credible sets explained 97 to 100% of significant marginal associations. Seven candidates were not reported by previous GTEx v8-based TWAS, including RIN3, supported only by APA, and NPAT for TNBC. Analyses across 48 tissues and brain cell types revealed brain contributions, including ARHGEF5 in oligodendrocytes. In African-ancestry populations, EN1 was prioritized for ER negative BC and TNBC through variants common in African but rare in European ancestry. These results refine BC susceptibility genes, highlight regulatory mechanisms beyond breast tissue and gene expression, and reveal the challenge of mapping GWAS variants to causal genes with currently available data.

papers.title: Complementary DNA-contact and domain-destabilizing mechanisms of PAX9 and MSX1 variants in non-syndromic tooth agenesis: an AlphaFold 3, ThermoMPNN, and AlphaGenome study
papers.abstract: Missense variants in the DNA-binding domains of PAX9 and MSX1 cause non-syndromic tooth agenesis, yet most substitutions remain variants of uncertain significance. We investigated the structural mechanisms of 39 pathogenic missense variants in the PAX9 paired domain (n = 32) and MSX1 homeodomain (n = 7) alongside 77 non-coding/splice ClinVar variants. We modelled protein-DNA complexes with AlphaFold 3, estimated folding stability changes ({Delta}{Delta}G) with ThermoMPNN, and compared pathogenic variants with gnomAD v4 domain variants. AlphaFold 3 confidence metrics and mutant interfaces were insensitive to point mutations. Instead, pathogenic PAX9 variants acted through two complementary mechanisms relative to recurrent population controls: loss of direct DNA contact ( 0.564) showed 8%-21% specificity across both domains. Mechanism did not predict missing teeth, whereas missense variants were milder than null alleles (p = 0.001). AlphaGenome matched SpliceAI and jointly prioritized seven intronic variants.

papers.title: Excess of de novo substitutions in the genomes of individuals with newly acquired germline TP53 mutations
papers.abstract: Inherited defects in the tumour suppressor gene TP53 cause Li-Fraumeni syndrome, a highly penetrant predisposition to childhood and adult cancers. About half of affected individuals carry a variant absent from both parents, and these are the patients missed by family-history-based testing criteria. Where and when such variants arise, in which parental gamete or after fertilisation, remains unresolved, as primary family data are scarce. We addressed this using whole-genome and linked-read sequencing of five family quartets, each comprising a proband with a confirmed newly arisen pathogenic TP53 variant, a closely age-matched unaffected sibling, and both parents, drawn from a cohort of 429 families meeting clinical criteria for the syndrome; matching for age controls for the strong dependence of mutation counts on parental age. Every proband carried a distinct heterozygous missense change in the DNA-binding domain of p53, and read-based phasing traced four of five to the paternal chromosome. Genome-wide, probands carried a significant excess of newly arisen single-nucleotide changes relative to their siblings, which persisted after correction for parental age and was detected on the paternal chromosome. No comparable excess was found for insertions, deletions, structural rearrangements or repeat expansions, and the excess mutations matched the two clock-like processes operating in all cells rather than any distinct mechanism. These features are hard to reconcile with an event confined to the parental germ cells, and instead point to TP53 variants that arise shortly after fertilisation and sweep the embryo, carrying neighbouring mutations with them. Consistent with such sweeps occurring throughout life, TP53 mutations in two large public tumour-genome collections were more clonal than other driver mutations, and the most clonal were present in more cells than the tumour itself, as expected when a cancer emerges within a pre-existing mutant patch of normal tissue. We propose that constitutional TP53 variants and these mutant patches form one continuum, distinguished principally by timing: a sweep during the first cleavage divisions produces a variant present throughout the body, whereas the same advantage acting later confines the clone to one tissue. This reframes a subset of Li-Fraumeni syndrome as an early developmental rather than strictly germline event, with implications for testing, counselling and surveillance.

papers.title: A new liability-based rare-variant burden test identifies a novel genetic association between HTRA3 and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
papers.abstract: In contrast to large-effect monogenic variants, which are highly penetrant regardless of genetic background, variants with more modest effect sizes depend on a carrier's genetic background to manifest disease. For many complex traits, including idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), polygenic risk scores (PRS) have been shown to capture a significant proportion of the genetic background risk. While a rare-variant association test incorporating a PRS covariate to account for the genetic background has been demonstrated to improve statistical power for gene discovery in quantitative traits, for binary traits, this approach shows limited or no power gain over PRS-unadjusted tests. Here, we propose a novel rare-variant association test for binary traits that jointly models the contribution of rare variants and PRS under a liability threshold model. In simulated datasets, our new method, liability threshold burden test (LTBT), shows a well-controlled false positive rate and outperforms the sensitivity of existing methods. To demonstrate this new method, we apply it to sequencing datasets for IPF, a rare but highly morbid lung disease. By accounting for an individual's genetic background with PRS, we identify and formally replicate a significant novel association of rare predicted damaging missense variants in HTRA3 (HtrA serine peptidase 3) with IPF.

papers.title: Combined genome-wide association studies in humans and cattle: Cross-species genetic insights into dizygotic twinning
papers.abstract: To leverage independent genetic evidence from multiple species, we developed a cross-species gene-based GWAS meta-analysis framework and applied this to Dizygotic Twinning (DZT) in humans and cattle. After meta-analysis within species, we converted human and cattle GWAS summary statistics to gene-level association signals within each species, mapped genes across species through human-cattle orthology, and then combined gene-level evidence for orthologous genes across the two species. DZT is defined as giving birth to multiple offspring after a single pregnancy resulting from spontaneous multiple ovulation. In humans, DZT occurs in about 1% of pregnancies with heritability estimates of 20% to 30% whilst in cattle DZT occurs in 1-5% of pregnancies and heritability is estimated at about 11%. Here, we present the largest human GWAS meta-analysis including data from 1,395,285 participants. We identified 16 genetic regions of interest, including 12 independent loci from the SNP based analyses and 4 genes identified in the gene-based MAGMA analyses. Among the prioritized genes are follicle stimulation hormone receptor (FSHR) and growth differentiation factor 9 (GDF9), that both are involved in ovarian folliculogenesis. Cattle GWAS summary statistics were based on data from 2,656 Irish Holstein bulls with estimated breeding values for predisposition to twinning based on 2,238,936 birth records, and 86,391 German Holstein dams. After combining the gene-level analyses for 13,225 genes mapped as orthologous across the human and cattle data we identify FSHR as a central locus for DZT in both humans and cattle. We find evidence of additional associations, including ACVR2A, which plays a role in embryonic implantation and TUFM, which has previously been implicated in premature ovarian insufficiency. Our approach provides a promising framework for future cross-species comparative GWAS studies. It shows benefits for gene discovery and gene prioritization and in our application expands available functional follow-up data, allowing us to leverage cattle eQTL data to resolve human GWAS loci. The method and underlying philosophy presented here are transferable to other shared phenotypes across several species.

papers.title: Mapping Gene-by-Environment Interactions via the Plasma Exposome at Cell-Type Resolution
papers.abstract: Gene-by-environment (GxE) interactions inform where genetics and environment converge to impact human health and disease. However, systematically mapping GxE interactions has been challenging due to the diversity of testable exposures and a lack of scalable approaches to measure the environments cells experience in vivo. Here, we identified modules of correlated plasma metabolites and proteins and used them as quantitative proxies for environmental exposures experienced by circulating leukocytes. We demonstrated that these proxies are associated with environmentally-modifiable clinical traits such as diet and infection and support broad mapping of gene-by-environment (G x E) interactions affecting gene expression and CpG methylation in leukocytes. We identified significant interactions for 95.2% of tested genes and 5.9% of tested methylation sites. These G x E interactions showed specificity to exposures and cell type. Colocalization analysis further provided links between interactions and complex trait and disease loci. Finally, we expanded G x E interaction mapping to unexplored cell types using a zero-shot transfer model to predict GxE interactions in held-out cell types, demonstrating how plasma metabolomics and proteomics can enhance the discovery of G x E interactions across the body. Altogether, this work provides a systematic multi-omic framework to study how gene regulation is shaped by both the genome and the molecular environments cells experience in vivo.

papers.title: Maternal vitamin D status during pregnancy is associated with reduced DNA methylation entropy and hypomethylation of regulatory regions related to immune tolerance
papers.abstract: BackgroundVitamin D is crucial to maternal immune system function during pregnancy, acting via the vitamin D receptor (VDR). Yet, there is widespread vitamin D insufficiency among pregnant women. The Vitamin D Antenatal Asthma Reduction Trial investigated maternal vitamin Ds effect on offspring asthma/wheeze. Pregnant women were randomized to a vitamin D supplementation or placebo group, and maternal blood samples were collected at 10-18 and 32-38 weeks of gestation. This analysis aims to identify associations between 25-hydroxyvitamin-D3 (25OHD) and DNA methylation (DNAm). DNAm data were obtained with Illuminas Infinium Methylation EPICv2 array. Linear mixed effects models assessed DNAm-25OHD associations, adjusting for demographic and clinical factors. Probe-level results were aggregated to identify differentially methylated regions (DMRs), which were annotated to genes via proximity to promoters or enhancers. In addition, DNAm entropy was investigated for associations with 25OHD. ResultsHypomethylated (meso-/hyper-methylated) DMRs showed negative (positive) DNAm-25OHD associations. DMRs overlapped with vitamin D-sensitive topologically associating domains and open chromatin. Annotated genes were primarily enriched for pathways related to antigen processing/presentation. Using paired RNA-seq data, the expression of 59 annotated genes was significantly associated with DNAm of its corresponding DMR. These included IKBKB, a kinase with suppressive effects on the NF-kappa-B pathway. Furthermore, DMRs showed negative entropy-25OHD associations, suggesting a more homogeneous immune methylome in women with higher 25OHD levels. ConclusionsOur findings suggest that increased vitamin D may promote methylome stability in genomic regions associated with antigen presentation and immune tolerance, conveying a complex regulatory landscape of the vitamin D-associated methylome during pregnancy.

papers.title: Transparent Implementation and Benchmarking of ACMG/AMP Variant Classification in fastVEP
papers.abstract: BackgroundThe ACMG/AMP framework is the standard for germline sequence variant interpretation, but applying it in scalable automated software requires operational choices that the original framework and later ClinGen guidance do not always specify. We implemented an ACMG/AMP classification engine within fastVEP and evaluated which implementation choices improved agreement with expert-curated classifications without increasing concerning opposite-direction calls. MethodsThe classifier implements all 28 ACMG/AMP criteria and can evaluate 15 from a sites-only VCF using nine public evidence sources. For selecting the optimal classifier, we compared symmetric and hybrid evidence-combining schemes, pathogenic class cutoffs, population-frequency thresholds, and benign-evidence thresholds against 673,660 ClinVar variants with review status of two stars or higher from April 2026. Clinical geneticists reviewed opposite-direction calls. We then applied the selected final classifier unchanged to 116,078 variants that newly reached the two-star threshold in the October 2026 ClinVar release. ResultsThe final fastVEP ACMG/AMP classifier uses the Tavtigian point scale on the pathogenic side and the 2015 ACMG/AMP combining table on the benign side. Using the 2015 table on both sides reduced pathogenic-side recall from 62.5 to 57.1 percent and lost 4,900 same-direction calls while avoiding 10 opposite-direction pathogenic calls. Using points on both sides increased benign-side recall from 66.4 to 77.0 percent, but increased opposite-direction benign calls from 27 to 399 and reduced recall of ClinVar uncertain variants from 97.1 to 69.5 percent. The 6-point Likely pathogenic cutoff was retained because lowering it to 5 points increased pathogenic-side recall to 73.9 percent but also classified 6,003 additional ClinVar uncertain variants and 17 additional ClinVar benign-side variants as pathogenic-side. The final classifier reproduced ClinVars exact five-tier class for 431,727 variants or 64.1 percent and its pathogenic, benign, or uncertain direction for 534,335 variants or 79.3 percent. Only 51 calls or 0.0076 percent were opposite in direction to ClinVar. On the later variants, same-direction agreement was 72.6 percent and 20 calls were opposite in direction. ConclusionsThe rules used to combine evidence affected classification more than several individual numeric thresholds. The hybrid scheme increased pathogenic-side recall while preventing a single Supporting benign criterion from producing a directional call. This conservative operating profile is suited to large-scale variant triage because it makes high-confidence calls while leaving variants uncertain when the available evidence does not support expert-level resolution. fastVEP is a research and decision-support tool and does not replace case-specific expert review.

papers.title: Prospective multi-omic profiling identifies predictive and genetically supported molecular determinants of incident epilepsy
papers.abstract: Epilepsy affects approximately 50 million people worldwide, yet biomarkers capable of identifying individuals at risk before clinical onset are lacking, and the molecular mechanisms preceding disease onset remain poorly understood. Here, we integrated plasma proteomic, metabolomic, and genomic data from the UK Biobank to characterize molecular changes preceding epilepsy and evaluate their predictive and causal relevance. We quantified 2,923 plasma proteins in [~]53,000 participants and followed incident epilepsy for up to 15 years before epilepsy diagnosis. Cox proportional hazards analyses identified 116 proteins associated with incident epilepsy, led by neurofilament light chain (NEFL; HR=2.03) and growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF15; HR=1.73). These proteins were enriched for extracellular signaling, immune regulation, and cell-death pathways and displayed distinct subtype-and age-specific signatures. A proteomic risk score comprising 32 proteins stratified epilepsy risk, with individuals in the highest quintile exhibiting a 3.5-fold greater risk than those in the lowest quintile (AUC=0.70). In parallel, 154 of 249 circulating metabolites were associated with incident epilepsy, with the strongest inverse association observed for citrate (HR=0.72) and positive associations across HDL-related metabolites (HR=1.16-1.21), implicating dysregulated energy and lipoprotein metabolism. A metabolomic risk score showed more modest discrimination (AUC=0.63). Integrating proteomic, metabolomic, polygenic, and demographic information yielded an overall AUC of 0.71 for incident epilepsy; in a separate cross-sectional analysis of individuals with early-onset epilepsy discrimination reached an AUC of 0.79. Proteome-wide cis-pQTL Mendelian randomization identified 12 proteins associated with epilepsy after false discovery rate correction, predominantly for genetic generalized epilepsy. O-GlcNAcase (OGA), a regulator of protein O-GlcNAcylation with established roles in neuronal function and synaptic plasticity, showed the strongest protective association (OR=0.71, FDR=2.7x10-). Serine protease 53 (PRSS53), a poorly characterized serine protease, showed strong evidence for a potential shared causal variant with epilepsy (colocalization PP.H4=0.95). Together, these findings demonstrate that circulating molecular alterations precede epilepsy diagnosis by years and reveal complementary proteomic, metabolic, and genetic determinants of disease susceptibility, providing a framework for biologically informed risk stratification and therapeutic target prioritization.

papers.title: Exome-wide rare-variant associations vary across disease trajectories
papers.abstract: Genetic studies of chronic disease typically collapse longitudinal clinical histories into binary case-control outcomes, obscuring disease timing and differences in genetic association patterns across disease transitions. Time-to-event analysis can preserve this information, but rare-variant analysis of post-diagnosis progression is challenged by sparse carrier-events and extensive censoring. We developed GATE-GENE, a scalable gene-based framework that maintains calibration under these conditions. Across 300 onset phenotypes in UK Biobank (UKB), GATE-GENE identified 107 exome-wide significant germline associations involving 89 genes and 67 diseases. Across 95 multi-state trajectories comprising baseline (T0), an upstream disease state (T1) and a downstream disease state (T2), disease onset (T0[->]T1) and subsequent progression (T1[->]T2) showed limited detectable sharing of rare-variant association signals. Progression showed greater concordance of gene-level association signals with downstream phenotypes (T0[->]T2) when the analyses shared T2 events occurring after T1. Removing overlapping downstream events reduced the median correlation between gene-level association signals from 0.063 to 0.001, after accounting for background correlation. Null simulations reproduced the relationship between event overlap and concordance without genetic effects, whereas additional simulations showed that near-zero concordance could persist despite extensive underlying causal-gene sharing. This attenuation was reproduced across three ancestry groups in All of Us. Cross-biobank meta-analysis identified 12 additional exome-wide significant progression associations beyond three UKB discoveries, although clinical sensitivity analyses suggested that the strongest PKD1 signals largely reflected underlying cystic kidney disease. Together, these findings establish GATE-GENE for investigating rare-variant associations with disease timing and progression, while demonstrating how overlapping clinical events and limited carrier-event information complicate inference about genetic sharing across disease transitions.

papers.title: Dual-platform plasma proteogenomics prioritizes GSTA1 and ARG1 as druggable cross-domain targets in cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome
papers.abstract: BackgroundCardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome reflects shared pathophysiology across metabolic, renal and cardiovascular systems, yet circulating proteins with causal effects spanning multiple CKM domains remain unclear. We aimed to identify and prioritize cross-domain candidate proteins using an integrative, dual-platform plasma proteogenomic framework. MethodsWe combined genetic causal inference, statistical colocalization, single-cell expression mapping, and structure-based druggability assessment. Cis-protein quantitative trait loci (cis-pQTL) instruments were derived from two independent plasma proteomic platforms, UKB-PPP (2,030 proteins with valid cis instruments) and deCODE (1,640 proteins). Genetic causal inference (two-sample Mendelian randomization) was performed against seven CKM-related outcomes across the metabolic (type 2 diabetes [T2D], body mass index [BMI]), renal (estimated glomerular filtration rate [eGFR], chronic kidney disease) and cardiovascular (coronary artery disease, heart failure, stroke) domains. Proteins showing false discovery rate (FDR)-significant associations in at least two CKM domains independently on both platforms were prioritized, and cross-platform directional concordance was evaluated as a robustness measure. Prioritized proteins were followed by colocalization, and characterization using single-cell expression, disease-association and druggability resources. Structural and ligand-efficiency analyses were performed for the leading candidate using its co-crystallized inhibitor complex. ResultsProteome-wide analysis yielded 9,734 (UKB-PPP) and 8,837 (deCODE) protein-outcome estimates, with 77.9% two-platform directional concordance. Cross-domain prioritization identified six proteins (ARG1, GSTA1, INHBB, ITIH1, NCAN, SHBG), all acting across the metabolic-renal axis. Colocalization provided strong support for GSTA1 with eGFR (posterior probability of a shared causal variant 0.97) and ARG1 with BMI (0.93). Genetically higher GSTA1 was associated with lower eGFR and higher T2D risk, with kidney expression confined to proximal tubule cells. Genetically higher ARG1 was associated with lower BMI and lower T2D risk, consistent with hepatocyte-restricted expression. Both proteins were small-molecule tractable. For GSTA1, the inhibitor-bound structure (PDB 1GSF) showed a deep, enclosed H-site, and three chemotypes with previously reported low-micromolar potency against recombinant hGSTA1-1 (ethacrynic acid and the dietary flavonols fisetin and myricetin) all exceeded the lead-like ligand-efficiency threshold (0.30 kcal mol-1 per heavy atom). ConclusionsUsing dual-platform proteogenomics, we identify genetically supported cross-metabolic-renal candidate proteins in CKM syndrome, with GSTA1 and ARG1 emerging as the most robust, pharmacologically tractable candidates. These findings nominate actionable targets and mechanistic entry points for CKM syndrome.

papers.title: Single-cell lung eQTL colocalization implicates alveolar epithelial regulatory effects at COPD lung-function loci
papers.abstract: BackgroundChronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and lung function are highly heritable, but for most genome-wide association study (GWAS) loci, the effector gene and the lung cell type in which it acts are unknown. Single-cell expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) offer a way to resolve the cell types in which regulatory variants act. ResultsWe integrated a multi-ancestry GWAS of the ratio of forced expiratory volume in one second to forced vital capacity (FEV1/FVC; Shrine et al., n = 588,452) with single-cell lung eQTLs across 38 cell types (Natri et al., n = 114) by colocalization. We identified 20 candidate colocalizations (posterior probability of a shared causal variant > 0.7) for 13 genes in nine cell types, predominantly epithelial and immune. The two strongest signals localized DSP, an established COPD effector gene, and NRP2, a candidate effector gene, to alveolar type 2 epithelial cells; only these two colocalizations remained supported under a more conservative shared-effect prior. Both signals, together with FAM13A, were also detectable in bulk lung eQTLs, whereas most remaining loci colocalized only in the single-cell analysis. ConclusionsSingle-cell eQTL colocalization resolves the alveolar epithelium as a cellular context for DSP and nominates NRP2 as a candidate lung function effector gene in the same compartment, highlighting the additional cellular resolution provided by single-cell data. The remaining candidate colocalizations warrant replication.

papers.title: The contribution of Neanderthal ancestry to cancer risk
papers.abstract: Modern human genomes harbor DNA inherited from interbreeding with Neanderthals. Genetic variants inherited from Neanderthals associate with variation in many immune and metabolic phenotypes, two systems with direct relevance to cancer. However, the influence of Neanderthal variants on germline cancer risk has not been comprehensively evaluated. Here, we evaluated genome-wide association study (GWAS) hits for 17 cancer types for Neanderthal ancestry. Twelve cancers have multiple Neanderthal alleles significantly associated with variation in risk. Next, we fine-mapped these risk loci and identified 32 associations across seven cancers where Neanderthal variants are likely causal ([≥] 50% posterior inclusion probability). Fine-mapped loci include Neanderthal alleles that both increase and decrease cancer risk. Nine of the 32 Neanderthal associations, including the high frequency BNC2 Neanderthal variants, have signatures of adaptive introgression, and several suggest evidence of both mediated and antagonistic pleiotropy. Finally, we tested for enrichment of cancer heritability in genomic regions with Neanderthal ancestry. As expected, Neanderthal variants are depleted of heritability for most cancers. However, Neanderthal variants were enriched for heritability in breast cancer GWAS in both East Asian and Europeans, and this enrichment replicated using individual-level UK Biobank data. These results suggest that Neanderthal alleles that influence germline cancer risk were largely selected against. However, introgressed Neanderthal variants implicated in many cancers persist, potentially due to adaptive pleiotropic effects. This evolutionary perspective provides new insights into the complex evolution and etiology of cancer risk among modern human populations.

papers.title: Gene-based map of cardiovascular diseases
papers.abstract: BackgroundRare coding variants contribute to cardiovascular disease, but their effects across disease groups remain incompletely characterized. In particular, the influence of functionally and clinically informed variant classification and sex-specific genetic effects on gene-phenotype associations remains understudied. MethodsWe analyzed whole-genome sequencing data from up to 483,311 UK Biobank participants across six genetic ancestry groups and eight cardiovascular phenotype groups. Gene-burden testing integrated state-of-the-art missense classification and predicted pathogenic germline variants. We performed combined-sex and sex-stratified analyses, followed by cross-ancestry meta-analysis. We additionally adjusted for cardiometabolic traits in sensitivity analyses, estimated penetrance among qualifying-variant carriers, and assessed genetic prevalence across eight ancestry groups. ResultsWe identified 86 exome-wide significant gene-phenotype associations: 40 established and 46 novel. Novel associations included EHMT2 with atrial fibrillation, P2RX1 with arrhythmias, P2RY4 with complete atrioventricular block, and NOSTRIN with atherosclerotic heart disease in females. After cardiometabolic adjustment, 60 associations retained exome-wide significance and 18 additional associations emerged, including CDH11, PARVA, and ADAMDEC1 with atherosclerosis-related phenotypes. ConclusionsThese findings identify novel cardiovascular gene-phenotype associations implicating purinergic signaling, endothelial nitric oxide regulation, and vascular wall biology. Variant selection shapes penetrance estimates and the interpretation of inherited susceptibility.

papers.title: "Wow, this could be massive": Donor-Conceived Families Experience with Unexpected Recontact for Risk of Inherited Cardiac Conditions
papers.abstract: IntroductionRecontacting families post-gamete donation, after a genetic diagnosis is made in the donor, can create complex challenges for healthcare providers and families. However, there is little literature that explores the family experience. This study aimed to explore the experiences of parents and donor-conceived young people navigating the recontact process and undergoing predictive genetic testing for an inherited cardiac condition. MethodsSemi-structured interviews were conducted to explore participants experiences in unexpectedly being recontacted and undergoing predictive genetic testing for an inherited cardiac condition. Interviews were recorded and transcribed verbatim. A reflexive thematic analysis was performed. ResultsThirteen participants agreed to be interviewed, nine were parents and four were donor conceived young people. Four overarching themes were identified: (1) Out of the Blue, (2) A ripple effect on the family, (3) Calm after the storm, (4) Beneath the Ripples: the psychological impact. DiscussionInterviews provided insights into fertility services recontact and the predictive genetic testing process. From the themes, we conceptualize a ripple effect model. Findings highlight how cardiac genetics and fertility services are evolving, and the critical role of genetic counselors. The recontact process affects the entire family. However, most participants adapted and moved forward from this event.

papers.title: How inherited variation shapes human disease trajectories
papers.abstract: Although inherited variation is fixed at birth, its effects on health change with age and differ between common and rare variants. Here, we introduce Mendelnoulli, a longitudinal model that combines the age-dependent effects of polygenic and monogenic variation on health records, separating the overall disease accumulation of each individual from the diseases to which they are prone. Mendelnoulli further allows polygenic and monogenic components to exert different influences on latent disease trajectories. We apply the model to 348 diseases, 36 polygenic scores, and 34 monogenic conditions across three biobanks and provide an atlas of the age-dependent effects of inherited variation on common human diseases. We show that polygenic effects change significantly with age. Mendelnoulli improved held-out one-year discrimination for all 28 diseases tested compared with a model whose polygenic effects are constant across age (mean AUC gain 0.023). For individuals with no prior diagnoses, Mendelnoulli identified 8.6 more cases of every 100 new cases than that model, when each flagged the 5% at highest risk. For genes with an established disease, Mendelnoulli selected that disease for 27 of 30 genes and ranked it first for 17 (7 expected by chance), and recovered known differences in timing, such as earlier breast cancer effects for BRCA1 than BRCA2 (peak 48 vs 66 years). Mendelnoulli models common and rare genetic influences on disease trajectories jointly throughout the life course.

papers.title: The phenomic landscape of rare gain- and loss-of-function variation
papers.abstract: Current large-scale phenome-wide association studies do not distinguish between genetic variants with distinct functional consequences, despite evidence that gain-of-function (GoF) and loss-of-function (LoF) variants can produce different phenotypes. Consequently, the phenotypic consequences of variants stratified by predicted GoF and LoF effects have not been systematically characterized at scale. Here, we systematically analyzed rare predicted GoF and LoF variants in 18,214 genes across 1,244 binary and 202 quantitative traits using whole-exome sequencing and electronic health records from the Mount Sinai Million Health Discoveries Program, a phenotypically rich hospital-based biobank comprised of 50,067 participants, primarily representing African, Admixed American and European ancestries. We identified numerous established and previously unreported ancestry-specific and shared gene- and variant-level associations, many of which were supported by complementary evidence from both diagnostic phenotypes and clinical measurements. Proteomic evaluation of the previously unreported association between VNN1 LoF variants and body mass index in the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis revealed reduced circulating vanin-1 levels with LoF variants, which in turn were associated with body composition and additional cardiometabolic phenotypes. Functional stratification of predicted GoF and LoF variants revealed gene-trait associations that were attenuated when these variants were combined, demonstrating that traditional aggregation of variants with different functional effects can obscure association signals. These findings underscore the importance of incorporating predicted functional consequences into association analyses and establish a comprehensive resource linking exome-wide predicted GoF and LoF variants to the human phenome across ancestry-specific and multi-ancestry analyses.

papers.title: Cancer risk and survival outcomes in germline POT1 variant carriers
papers.abstract: BackgroundThe prevalence of germline POT1 variants, spectrum of associated tumors, cancer risk and survival outcomes are incompletely described, and clinical management guidelines vary. We evaluated POT1 variant carriers in three biobanks and a clinical cohort to address these limitations. MethodsPrevalence, cancer spectrum and risk associated with germline POT1 pathogenic/likely pathogenic and additional functionally assessed variants were evaluated in Penn Medicine Biobank (PMBB; n=51,172), Geisinger MyCode (MyCode; n=220,582), UK Biobank (UKBB; n=469,558) and a Penn Medicine clinical cohort. ResultsEstimated POT1 variant prevalence ranged from 1:1,279 to 1:2,902. Compared to non-carriers, cancer diagnoses were more frequent among POT1 variant carriers in PMBB (OR 3.41, 95%CI 1.81-6.43, p=1.88x10-4), MyCode (OR 2.23, 95%CI 1.31-3.79, p=0.003), and UKBB (OR 1.40, 95%CI 1.07-1.84, p=0.015). Cancer incidence increased beginning in the mid-30s, without evidence of increased mortality. Along with previously described cancer types, lung cancer was associated with POT1 variant carriers in two biobank cohorts. ConclusionPOT1 is a cancer susceptibility gene associated with a moderate (1.5-3.5-fold) increased cancer risk. Variants are relatively frequent and predispose to a broad tumor spectrum and increased incidence starting in the mid-30s, without increasing mortality. These findings expand understanding of POT1-associated disease and provide data to inform clinical management.

papers.title: Enrichment of Rare Exonic Variants in Cognitive Superagers from Centenarian Families
papers.abstract: While the risk of cognitive impairment and dementia increases with advanced age, a fraction of individuals maintains high levels of cognitive function at extreme ages. Here, we compared whole-exome sequencing variant frequency data for 136 centenarian and offspring cognitive superagers, whose episodic memory performance matches normative expectations for persons [~]30 years younger, 114 average-cognition controls, and the gnomAD population reference database. A rare variant allele frequency analysis identified 114 rare coding variants significantly enriched in cognitive superagers, of which the ten most significant variants were exceedingly rare missense variants residing in nine genes implicating neurovascular biology (LOX, CLEC4M, ZNG1F), immune regulation (HLA-B, HLA-DRB1, ITGAX, MUC4, MUC1), and neuronal structure (CEP131, two variants). Together, these findings support the study of an extreme phenotype as a tractable framework for prioritizing rare coding variation and nominating a set of candidate loci for functional follow-up to help elucidate protective genetic mechanisms in cognitive superagers.

papers.title: Genetic architecture and polygenic prediction of self-reported response to selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors in individuals with depression: a genome-wide meta-analysis
papers.abstract: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are first-line treatments for depression, but response is highly variable, and no robust genetic predictors have been identified. We conducted a genome-wide association meta-analysis of self-reported SSRI response in 62,879 individuals of European ancestry with depression (72.6% responders) across six cohorts (seven datasets), followed by gene-set, transcriptomic, proteomic, drug-target and polygenic score (PGS) analyses. SNP-based heritability was modest but significant (h{superscript 2} = 3.1%, SE = 1.4%) with no genome-wide significant variants detected. Gene-set analyses implicated gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA)ergic and glutamatergic neurotransmission, and a gene involved in glutamate transport (SLC17A6) showed consistent sub-threshold evidence across pathway, transcriptomic and proteomic analyses. Drug-target enrichment for hypnotics, anxiolytics and general anesthetics further supported the GABAergic signal. A leave-one-out PGS from the discovery meta-analysis was associated with self-reported SSRI response in independent cohorts (meta-analysis OR=1.05, 95% CI 1.02-1.08, p=0.002). Higher PGS for depression, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), autism, addiction and schizophrenia were associated with lower odds of reported SSRI response, with ADHD, PTSD, autism and addiction remaining after adjustment for depression PGS. In contrast, educational attainment PGS was associated with better SSRI response. Self-reported SSRI response captures genetic insights relevant to antidepressant response, implicating GABAergic and glutamatergic neurotransmission. Individuals with higher genetic loading for psychiatric conditions report poorer response, and higher genetic loading for educational attainment PGS a better reported response. Although larger studies are needed to identify specific variants, self-report offers a practical, patient-centered and scalable route to collect the larger samples required.
